demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette: The phone rings at 3:14 a.m. The dispatcher's voice is calm, detached, describing a rain-slicked curve of highway, a guardrail that gives way, and the quiet finality of a life extinguished in seconds. Elias hears his younger brother's name, hears the word unresponsive, and feels the floor tilt beneath his boots. He drives through a downpour he barely registers, his knuckles white on the steering wheel, rehearsing what he will say, what he will hold, how he will anchor the room. By the time he reaches the house, the silence is already absolute. He stands in the kitchen until the coffee goes cold, waiting for a phone to ring, for a door to open, for the world to correct itself. It does not. In the months that follow, Elias tries to rebuild his days the way he rebuilds his work: with deliberate pressure, with measured turns, coaxing structure from something that constantly wants to collapse. At sixty-two, he has spent nearly forty years at a potter's wheel. The studio on the edge of town smells of damp earth and mineral glaze. The wheel used to be his grounding. Now, centering the clay feels like a negotiation he keeps losing. His hands know the rhythm, but his mind fractures at the edge of each rotation. When the clay dips, when the piece wobbles, his breath catches. He stops. He scrapes the clay into a bucket, his jaw tight, and tells himself it is just water, just dust, just motion. But the tremor in his forearms does not fade. He avoids the kiln room. The sudden hiss of the gas igniter sends his pulse straight to his throat. He tells his wife, Clara, he is waiting for a new regulator, but she watches him wipe his hands on his apron until the cotton turns gray and damp. Sleep has become a territory he rarely wins. He lies awake past 2 a.m., listening to the house settle. Every creak, every draft against the windowframe, sounds like tires on wet asphalt. He checks the deadbolt three times. He reads the same page of his paperback four times, his eyes skimming words without absorbing them. When he dozes, he wakes with his heart hammering, certain he is late, certain something has already broken that he cannot stop. He does not tell Clara he wakes with his hand hovering over his chest, as if pressing down on a sudden, invisible weight. He just pours coffee, stands by the back door, and watches the street until his eyes burn. He arrives at our Tuesday appointments with the same measured步速. He brings blocks of greenware he leaves on his windowsill to split on their own. He says he likes watching them crack. "It is not failing," he tells me, voice low. "It is just releasing what it cannot hold." The symptom survey he completed last month tallies at sixty, but the number only maps the perimeter of his exhaustion. The real measure is in the way he flinches when the receptionist drops her keys, the way he scans the parking lot for familiar vehicles before stepping from his truck, the way he pauses mid-sentence when someone mentions the rain, the curve, the days since. His marriage remains intact but stretched thin. Clara reaches for him in the evenings; he retreats into routine, into the heavy, predictable resistance of wedging clay, into the precise, measurable act of trimming. He says he is working through it. His hands never fully believe him. Today, he sits back against the worn leather. The afternoon light slants across his work boots, still caked with dried slip. He does not look at me. He watches a hairline fracture spread across a drying bowl on the shelf near the door. "I keep expecting the wheel to catch me," he says. "But it doesn't. It just keeps spinning." He exhales, slow and even, and folds his hands over his knees. The session continues.
